title: Intro: Redwood Console — route economics & per-route cost walkthrough

transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-05-02 11:00 AM PT
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood CSM), Lena (Cedarbridge Eng Mgr), Owen (Cedarbridge DevOps), Marisol (Head of AI), Samir (Security), Ethan (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood demo focusing on Console route economics. Showed per-route cost lenses, token-level attribution, routing fallbacks and private options. Customer asked about data residency, SOC2, and how to map costs to product teams. Agreed to pilot two routes, run benchmarks, and exchange security docs.

Topics covered:
- Console: usage overview and per-route dashboards
- Token breakdown and per-route chargeback
- Routing policies, canary & fallback to cheaper variants
- Dedicated capacity and Private (VPC) options
- Security and compliance (SOC2, SSO, KMS)
- Pilot plan and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. Diego, you wanna quick 1-liner?
[00:06] Diego: Yeah hi, Diego Alvarez, SE, I'll run through the console demo and then we can dig into perf and security stuff as needed.
[00:12] Lena: Hi, sorry ran a sec late — Lena here, Engineering manager at Cedarbridge. We're mostly focused on two product routes that are driving most of our spend.
[00:20] Ethan: And hi, Ethan from product. We'll want to see mapping to features not just token counts.
[00:25] Maya: Great. Quick agenda: show the Console usage dashboard -> per-route cost views -> routing/fallbacks -> then dedicated/private options and security. We'll leave 10 minutes to nail down pilot next steps.
[00:36] Owen: Sounds good. We have questions about how token attribution works when we use caching and when we do partial prompts.
[00:42] Diego: Totally, that's a good one. We'll show an example with prefix caching and the KV cash — sorry, KV cache — where you see the reused tokens deducted from the per-route unit. Sometimes transcription shows 'cash' for cache in our exports, but that's just the auto-t.
[00:56] Marisol: One thing up front, we have strict residency reqs, and encryption at rest must be customer KMS. Can Redwood support bringing your own K-M-S?
[01:06] Maya: Yes — for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS and HSMs, and Dedicated can be configured with customer-managed keys. We'll share the security whitepaper after.
[01:13] Samir: Also need audit logs and per-token tracer, like who called which route and which model version — is that available?
[01:20] Diego: Yes, we have token-level traces and request-level metadata you can export. The Console also has route-level traces that link back to request ids for auditing.
[01:29] Diego: Ok, I'll jump into screen share — tell me if the stream stutters.
[01:35] [screen share starts]
[01:40] Diego: This is the Console home. Topline is overall usage and cost burn, then down here we have 'Routes' which is where you can split by product surface. For Cedarbridge you'd create a route per product flow — e.g., 'payments-verification' and 'customer-chat' — and the Console will map tokens, latency, and cost per route.
[01:58] Lena: Can we tag routes with teams and Jira projects? We want to do chargeback by team.
[02:04] Diego: Yep, you can add tags and owner metadata to each route. The dashboards can pivot on tags, owner, and model. We'll show a cost-per-team view in a sec.
[02:12] Diego: Here is a per-route timeline — you can see token consumption, average latency, and cost per minute. The cost is token-level multiplied by model price and adjusted for batching and KV cache hits.
[02:26] Ethan: Quick Q: How do you handle partial prompt reuse? For us, some prompts have static context + dynamic user text, and we only want to charge the dynamic tokens.
[02:34] Diego: We support prefix/k-v caching and prefix reuse so you only pay for the new generation tokens. In the Console it shows 'reused tokens' as a negative adjustment on the per-route ledger. Sometimes the auto-transcript will say K-V cash but it's cache.
[02:47] Marisol: Is the reuse automatic or do we need to annotate prompts?
[02:51] Diego: It works with the runtime automatically if you configure the route to keep KV caches and you pass a stable prefix. For advanced cases we have SDK helpers.
[02:58] Owen: Ok nice. What about cost drift alerts? We want to be notified if a route's spend per week goes up 30%.
[03:04] Diego: You can set alerts on percent delta, absolute spend, or token rate. Alerts can notify Slack, PagerDuty, or email and can trigger an automated fallback to a cheaper model variant while you debug.
[03:16] Lena: Fallbacks sound useful — can we do canary releases where a percentage of traffic goes to a new model?
[03:21] Diego: Yes exactly. Rollouts support canary, A/B, and weight-based routing. You can route by latency SLOs, cost per token, or region. If the canary fails, we auto-fallback to the previous version or to a cheaper variant.
[03:34] Ethan: How fine-grained is the cost allocation? We need to bill different product teams.
[03:39] Maya: The Console gives you per-route, per-team, per-model breakdowns. You can export CSVs for chargeback. There's also a 'cost attribution' view that maps tokens to product tags.
[03:48] [05:00ish cross-talk, someone muted/unmuted]
[04:10] Samir: On compliance, what's in the audit trail? We need tamper-proof logs for requests and key events.
[04:16] Diego: We stream audit logs to your S3 or logging endpoint, and logs include request ids, route, model version, token counts, and the auth principal. For tamper-proofing, some customers put logs into an append-only store or SIEM — we support integration with common SIEMs.
[04:30] Marisol: Any latency numbers for large language models on Redwood Dedicated? Our SLO is 300ms P95 for 512-token responses.
[04:38] Diego: On dedicated pools with A100-grade hardware and our batching kernel selection we routinely hit sub-200ms P95 for short responses; for 512 tokens it's a function of model and batch. We showed benchmarks in the onboarding doc but we can run a targeted bench.
[04:50] Lena: Do you support quantized models to save cost?
[04:53] Diego: Yes, we support quant quantization profiles and will recommend quantization vs FP16 depending on quality constraints. The Console Optimize tab has suggestions per route: quantize this model, increase batch size, or enable prefix caching.
[05:06] Ethan: Can we preview the suggested unit cost savings if we enable those?
[05:09] Diego: Yup, it simulates the unit cost impact and shows historical projected savings.
[05:15] Maya: I want to call out the 'per-route cost lens' — it's useful for product managers to see the top cost drivers (model choice, sequence length, failed retries, and warmup traffic).
[05:26] Diego: Here's the route detail for 'payments-verification' — volume, tokens per call, average response length, and the cost waterfall. The waterfall shows model compute cost, rounding, and batching credits. There's also a chart that attributes cost to the model variant and to KV cache savings.
[05:43] Samir: If we go Private in a VPC, can we keep the same Console UX? We don't want to change the flow for product teams.
[05:50] Maya: Yes, the Console is available as a private control plane. UX is the same, you just host the control plane in your VPC and we connect the serving plane. The APIs and route configs are identical.
[05:59] Marisol: Any special networking requirements for Private?
[06:02] Diego: Minimal: outbound to a control plane endpoint if you want managed telemetry, or fully air-gapped if you want an on-prem package — we have an on-prem option. We'll share the network wiring doc.
[06:14] Lena: On the pricing side, how do burst capacity and reserved Dedicated pools interplay? We have spiky traffic during month-end.
[06:20] Maya: Dedicated is reserved for predictable baseline throughput. You can add burst capacity that bills at a premium per token or you can set routing to fall back to Hosted during spikes. Pricing sheet will show the breakpoints.
[06:32] Owen: Is there an easy way to measure cost per feature such that the finance team can bill back product teams?
[06:36] Diego: The 'chargeback export' provides daily breakdown per route with tags and cost columns ready for ingestion to your finance system. You can map to internal cost centers or Jira projects.
[06:46] Ethan: Do you have examples of customers who've migrated from internal self-hosting and saved money?
[06:51] Maya: Yep, we have case studies — often the savings come from smarter batching, caching, and switching to model variants for low-risk routes. We'll link to a couple of anonymized case studies.
[07:02] Marisol: Security again: we need SSO/SAML with SCIM user provisioning, RBAC, and separation of duties.
[07:10] Priya: We support SSO via SAML and OIDC, SCIM provisioning for users, and RBAC that can be scoped to routes. We can demo the RBAC screen in a follow-up.
[07:19] Samir: For data retention, we want to ensure that PII never leaves our VPC. If we use Hosted for some routes, how do you guarantee that?
[07:29] Diego: For PII you'd typically run those routes on Private or Dedicated with customer-managed keys and disable logs or redact payloads. We can also set routing rules so certain prompt patterns go to private endpoints.
[07:42] Lena: That routing by content — is that runtime inspect? We need to avoid latency spikes.
[07:46] Diego: It's done at the routing layer with light-weight matching; it adds minimal latency, and you can pre-compile rules. For very low-latency needs we recommend keeping it in Dedicated/Private.
[07:58] [10:00 - demo continues, Diego clicks through some panels]
[08:15] Diego: Here's the 'Optimize' suggestions for a route — it lists candidate optimizations, expected cost delta, and confidence score. For payments-verification it suggests 4-bit quantization of model-x with estimated 23% cost reduction and low risk to accuracy.
[08:33] Marisol: What's the fallback if quantization lowers accuracy?
[08:36] Diego: You can set quality regressions monitors — if evaluation metrics drop on a sample prompt set, the system can automatically revert or shift traffic back to a higher fidelity variant.
[08:48] Ethan: For the pilot, we want to measure real user latencies and token costs across our flows. What does Redwood need from us?
[08:56] Diego: We'll need two routes identified, sample traffic or synthetic traces, expected P95 goals, and a list of prompt templates. We'll run bench runs and provide the console telemetry.
[09:06] Lena: Timeline for pilot?
[09:08] Maya: We proposed a two-week pilot starting approx May 10th, benchmark in week 1, production shadow in week 2, then review.
[09:16] Samir: We'll confirm internal approvals by Friday.
[09:19] Marisol: One more question: can we export per-request payloads for debugging? We have to be careful with PII.
[09:25] Priya: You can export request metadata and token counts; exporting full payloads is optional and we recommend redaction. We can provide a sanitized debug stream.
[09:36] Owen: Any concerns when mixing models across routes? For example, one route uses a smaller 3B model and another uses a 70B. Any gotchas?
[09:43] Diego: The Console surfaces inconsistencies: per-token price, latency expectations, and you can set route-level SLOs. The runtime will route based on policy; mixed model fleets are common.
[09:54] [10:00] Maya: Ok let's wrap with next steps. Diego, you want to summarize pilot deliverables?
[10:05] Diego: Sure. We'll draft a pilot plan: what data we need, performance script, and success criteria (latency P95 threshold, cost per call target, and no regression on quality). I'll also include a KV cache warmup step to avoid cold-start noise.
[10:18] Maya: I'll send pricing and the SOC2 & security docs. Samir, you'll share the residency and compliance checklist.
[10:25] Samir: Yes, we'll get that over.
[10:28] Lena: If we like the pilot results, what's the typical timeline to migrate a small set of routes to Dedicated?
[10:33] Maya: Typically 4-8 weeks depending on infra approvals and network setup. If you're already cloud-ready it tends toward the 4-week end.
[10:40] Ethan: Great. Anything else?
[10:42] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the pilot plan and a calendar invite for kickoff.
[10:47] [meeting ends]

End notes: The transcript has the usual auto-caption quirks (e.g., K-V cash -> KV cache, Red wood -> Redwood). Links mentioned during call: security whitepaper (link shared after), pilot plan doc (to be shared), pricing sheet (to be shared).
